---
title: "Exercises — Anatomy of a library molecule"
---

Pen and paper. Draw the molecule first in every problem; most of the answers fall out of the
drawing. Sequences are from the TruSeq and Nextera adapters used in the deck.

# Part 1 — Reading a construct

## E1. Label this sequence

This is the 5′ end of the top strand of a TruSeq library, 70 bases long, before the insert:

`AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACTAGATCGCACACTCTTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT`

a. Which part is the P5 region, which the index, which the Read 1 site? Give base positions.
b. At which position does the insert begin, and at which cycle does Read 1 first read it?
c. The adapter has a Y shape. Which letters of this strand take part in the stem?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
The P5 region is 29 bases and the index is 8. The stem is the last stretch of the Read 1 site
that is complementary to the other arm: the 12 bp stem plus the T overhang.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. P5 is positions 1–29 (`AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACAC`), the index is 30–37 (`TAGATCGC`), and
   the Read 1 site is 38–70 (`ACACTCTTTCCCTACACGACGCTCTTCCGATCT`, 33 bases).
b. The insert begins at position 71. Read 1 starts right after the primer site, so cycle 1
   reads base 71 of this strand, the first base of the insert.
c. The last 13 bases, `GCTCTTCCGATCT`: 12 pair with the other arm, and the final T is the 3′
   overhang that pairs with the insert's A.
:::

## E2. From construct to read structure

A construct reads, left to right:
P5 – i5 (8) – Read 1 site – cell barcode (12) – UMI (8) – insert – Read 2 site – i7 (8) – P7.

You want the cell barcode, the UMI and 56 bases of insert in Read 1, 56 bases of insert in
Read 2, and both sample indexes. Give the read structure as R1 / I1 / I2 / R2.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Read 1 runs from the primer site over the barcode, the UMI and into the insert:
12 + 8 + 56 = 76 cycles. Index 1 is i7: 8. Index 2 is i5: 8. Read 2 is 56.
Read structure `76 / 8 / 8 / 56`. The first 20 bases of Read 1 are not genome, and the
analysis must be told so.
:::

## E3. From read structure to construct

A protocol is run as `20 / 10 / 10 / 80`. Read 1 is an 8-base well barcode followed by a
12-base UMI. Draw the construct. Where does the insert have to be read from?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
P5 – i5 (10) – Read 1 site – well barcode (8) – UMI (12) – insert – Read 2 site – i7 (10) – P7.
Read 1 covers only the barcode and the UMI and stops before the insert, so the **whole
insert information comes from Read 2**, read from the Read 2 side. Read 1 contains
nothing from the genome, and the pipeline must be told so.
:::

# Part 2 — Why the architecture looks like this

## E4. Why not two straight adapters?

A colleague proposes ligating a mixture of a P5-type adapter A and a P7-type adapter B, instead
of a Y adapter, "to save on oligo cost". Both are added in equal amounts and ligate at random.

a. What fraction of molecules has P5 at one end and P7 at the other?
b. What does this predict for the yield of clusterable library?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. Each end is A or B with probability ½, independently: A/A ¼, B/B ¼, A/B or B/A ½.
   Only the mixed molecules carry both a P5 and a P7 end.
b. At most half the library clusters, even in the ideal case. The Y adapter makes every
   end carry both arms, so no molecule is lost to the wrong combination.
:::

## E5. How many Nextera fragments are usable?

Tn5 is loaded with tag A and tag B in a ratio of 1 : 1 and tags each end independently.
Only A/B fragments become P5 … P7 molecules.

a. What fraction is usable?
b. What if the loading is 3 : 1?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
If a fraction p of ends carries tag A, a fragment is A/B with probability 2p(1 − p).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. p = ½, so 2 × ½ × ½ = 50 %.
b. p = ¾, so 2 × ¾ × ¼ = 37.5 %.
Even loading is best. The real kit does not say what its ratio is, so treat these as the
shape of the problem, not a prediction.
:::

## E6. Why does Nextera XT start its PCR with 72 °C?

After tagmentation, each strand carries a tag on its 5′ end and the DNA has a 9-nt gap. A
primer for tag A has the sequence of the tag. Why must the 3′ ends be extended before
the first denaturation, and what happens if you skip it?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
A primer with the sequence of the tag anneals to the **complement** of the tag. That complement
does not exist yet: the tag is a single-stranded 5′ flap on one strand, and the opposite strand
ends 9 bases short of it. The 72 °C step lets the polymerase extend the recessed 3′ end across
the gap and copy the tag, which creates the primer binding site. Without it the first PCR
cycles have no template for the primers and yield falls.
:::

## E7. Full adapters or truncated adapters?

Choose, and say which property of the molecule decides it.

a. 2 µg of human genomic DNA, 30× coverage, no wish for PCR duplicates or GC bias.
b. 96 samples of 1–5 ng each, from a plate.
c. The same as (b), but you must be certain that no index is swapped.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. **Full adapters, PCR-free** (TruSeq DNA PCR-free): the input is high enough and the
   ligation delivers the finished molecule. Quantify by qPCR.
b. **Truncated adapters or tagmentation with index PCR**: the input is far too low to go
   without amplification, and the indexes are installed by the PCR primers.
c. Still (b), with **unique dual indexes** and a thorough clean-up: swapping comes from free
   adapter or primer in the pool, whichever architecture is used.
:::

# Part 3 — What goes wrong

## E8. A peak at 135 bp

A library Bioanalyzer trace shows the expected 400 bp peak and a clear peak at about 135 bp.
The library is a TruSeq-style one with 8-base indexes.

a. Which molecule is it? Explain the size from the parts of the molecule.
b. What do the reads from these clusters look like?
c. Why is a *small* amount of it harmful?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. An adapter dimer: both adapter oligos ligated with no insert. P5 (29) + i5 (8) + Read 1
   site (33) on one arm and 33 + 8 + 24 on the other: 70 + 65 = 135 bp.
b. Adapter from the first cycle: Read 1 runs straight into the other arm's sequence,
   past the index and into P7′, and Read 2 does the same. The molecule ends well before
   the read does.
c. Short molecules cluster more efficiently, so the dimers take a bigger share of the
   clusters than of the molecules.
:::

## E9. An index inside Read 1

In a pool of short fragments, many Read 1 sequences end in
`…AGATCGGAAGAGCACACGTCTGAACTCCAGTCACTTAGGCATCTCGTATGCC`.

a. Which part of the construct has Read 1 reached?
b. Which index does it contain, and what will the Index 1 read of that cluster show?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. The insert is shorter than the read, so Read 1 has run through the Read 2 site
   (`AGATCGGAAGAGCACACGTCTGAACTCCAGTCAC`), then the index, then the P7 end.
b. The index is `TTAGGC`, between the Read 2 site and `ATCTCGTATGCC`. The Index 1 read of the
   same cluster shows `TTAGGC` as well, in the same orientation. It is a free check that the
   demultiplexing used the right orientation.
:::

# Self-check

1. Name the seven parts of an Illumina library molecule in order.
2. Which of them are fixed by the platform, which are chosen per sample, and which are yours?
3. What would go wrong with a straight adapter, and how does the Y adapter prevent it?
4. Why does Tn5 waste half of the fragments, and how is the rest recovered?
5. Given a construct, how do you derive the read structure, and how do you go back?
6. Which molecules in a tube do not cluster, and which cluster but give nothing?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. P5, i5, Read 1 site, insert, Read 2 site, i7, P7.
2. Fixed: P5, P7 and the two primer sites. Per sample: i5 and i7. Yours: the insert.
3. A straight adapter gives the same flow-cell end twice, so the molecule cannot bridge.
   The Y adapter has two different arms on every end, so every strand is P5 … P7.
4. Tags go on at random, so half of the fragments are A/A or B/B; only A/B pick up both an i5
   and an i7 primer in the tailed PCR. The rest does not cluster.
5. List the parts in order, draw a read arrow from each primer site, and count the bases it
   covers; the reverse is the same drawing read the other way.
6. No cluster: same end twice, one end only. Cluster but useless: adapter dimers, and
   inserts shorter than the read (adapter read-through). Poor: inserts that are too long.
:::
